title: Design for quiet living: A Science and Technology Studies perspective on architecture and noise mitigation policies

findings.antecedent: Visualizations (crafted in this study)
findings.consequent: Good legibility, efficacy in promoting new perspective on the process, increased interactions and clarifications among actors
findings.quote: The visualizations defined in this study resulted to have a good legibility and efficacy in promoting new perspective on the process by actors involved in it, as well as interactions and clarifications among such actors.

findings.antecedent: Visualizations (crafted in this study)
findings.consequent: Suitability for application on different case studies/contexts
findings.quote: They also resulted to be suitable for the application on a different case study from the one for which they were initially designed.

findings.antecedent: Major controversies arising after closing of first bureaucratic phases (Turin case)
findings.consequent: Higher number of local authorities involved, relatively small modification of the project (building itself)
findings.quote: the raising of the major number of controversies after the closing of the first bureaucratic phases in the case of Turin determined the involvement of a higher number of local authorities, including resolutions from the municipal board, while a relatively small modification of the project, and in particular of the building itself, derived from such complex exchanges.

findings.antecedent: Development of matters of concern before closing bureaucratic phases (Utrecht case)
findings.consequent: Limited number of human actors/organizations enrolled, important modifications in building design, integration of noise mitigation requirements
findings.quote: in the Utrecht case-study the development of all the matters of concern before the closing of the bureaucratic phases of the project determined the enrolment of a limited number of human actors and organizations in the concerns and on the other side a series of important modifications in the building design that allowed the integration of noise mitigation requirements.

findings.antecedent: Comprehensive strategy (including all requirements at initial stages, openness to modifications)
findings.consequent: Translation of different requirements into designs, stakeholder approval, avoidance of major concerns/long negotiations in later phases
findings.quote: a more comprehensive strategy which can include all the possible requirements and issues at the initial stages of the process, by complicating the process more at the beginning, when the openness of the project to modifications allows the translation of different requirements into designs which are approved by all the stakeholders, hence avoiding major concerns and long negotiations in the following phases.

findings.antecedent: Realization modalities of mitigation solutions at source
findings.consequent: Dependence on many different human/non-human actors, close connection to infrastructures/underground utilities
findings.quote: the concerns on realization modalities are related to mitigation solutions at source, as they depend from many different human and non-human actors apart from the proponent, as they are closely connected to the realization of infrastructures and underground utilities.

findings.antecedent: Requests of realization timing for mitigation solutions (e.g., noise reducing asphalt)
findings.consequent: Did not fit timing of building site, leading to strong controversies
findings.quote: Such controversies were strongly linked to requests of realization timing that, while trying to split the burden of mitigation solutions within the different allotments of the project, did not fit the timing of the building site (especially for noise reducing asphalt, see Chapter 6).

findings.antecedent: Late emerging of noise mitigation issues at receiver (when building design was fixed)
findings.consequent: Very small changes in the project, solutions could not be realized
findings.quote: the matters of concern related to noise mitigation at receiver determined very small changes in the project, as most of them could not be realized due to the late emerging of the issue, when the design of the building had already been fixed by the closing of previous bureaucratic phases.

findings.antecedent: Noise mitigation at receiver (involving building design), tackled at very first design stages
findings.consequent: Good solution, may not require extra time/agreement with other parties, integrated in building design/realization
findings.quote: noise mitigation at receiver, involving the design of the building, could be a good solution as they may not require extra time and agreement with other parties for their realization, since are integrated in the building design and realization. Of course, this requires to tackle the issue at the very first design stages.

findings.antecedent: Moving mitigation solutions to initial phases of project, including solutions at receiver
findings.consequent: Architect plays crucial role as mediator, reinforcing role in design process
findings.quote: By moving the issue of mitigation solutions to the initial phases of the project process and including mitigation solutions at the receiver, a crucial role of mediator between noise mitigation issues and other requirements could be played by the architect, reinforcing his role as part of the design process (Bradbury 2016).

findings.antecedent: Policies setting noise limits without prescriptive indications for mitigation solution design (Turin case)
findings.consequent: Policies did not have agency in defining mitigation solutions
findings.quote: in the Turin case-study, in which policies set requirements in terms of noise limits to be reached at all the facades of the building, without posing indications or prescriptions related to mitigation solution design, the policies did not have an agency in the matters of concern related to the definition of mitigation solutions.

findings.antecedent: Lack of normative requests on mitigation solutions at receiver + late tackling of issue (after design fixed)
findings.consequent: Architect not enrolled in noise mitigation issue
findings.quote: The lack of normative requests on mitigation solutions at receiver, together with the late tackling of the issue (after the design had already been fixed by the approval of the executive planning instrument) did not enrol the architect in the noise mitigation issue.

findings.antecedent: Lack of prescriptive indication on mitigation solutions (in new policy)
findings.consequent: Local Environment area and stakeholders defined praxis beyond legislation, acting as 'designer' of norms, transposed to other projects
findings.quote: the lack of prescriptive indication on mitigation solutions, in a newly-established policy, led to a “grey area” in which the local Environment area and the other involved stakeholders had to define praxis of action that go beyond legislation and were then transposed into other projects, hence acting as “designer” of norms, with the help of information from literature and from previous case-studies.

findings.antecedent: Contingent situation (requiring new modus operandi)
findings.consequent: Norms change (relational matrix between projects and norms)
findings.quote: not only the project changes because of normative requirements, but also the norms change because of a contingent situation that needs to establish a new modus operandi.

findings.antecedent: Integrated work and enhanced communication among local offices
findings.consequent: Different requirements do not lead to contradictory documents binding project aspects
findings.quote: the need for an integrated work and enhanced communication among the different local offices, so that different requirements do not lead to documents which bind aspects of the project that might be contradictory.

findings.antecedent: More data available, dissemination of practices (from environment agencies, practitioners, local offices), more academic research
findings.consequent: Support decisions, support local offices in similar decisions
findings.quote: the need to make more data available to support decisions and dissemination of practices. Hence, experiences from environment agencies, practitioners and local offices should be disseminated, and more academic research might be devoted to provide data and support local offices in similar decisions.

findings.antecedent: High level of detail in local noise policies/guidelines (building design, e.g., minimum silent façade dimension)
findings.consequent: Important role in matters of concern related to mitigation solutions at receiver (building design)
findings.quote: in the Utrecht case study the high level of detail with which local noise policies and guidelines on the topic of building design, defining indications and limits for it (e.g. minimum dimension of silent façade, etc.) led them to have an important role in the matters of concern related to mitigation solutions at receiver, hence to building design.

findings.antecedent: High level of detail in local noise policies/guidelines
findings.consequent: No 'grey areas', no relational matrix between norms and projects
findings.quote: The level of detail did not leave “grey areas” on this topic, hence no relational matrix between norms and projects was witnessed.

findings.antecedent: Local noise policies/guidelines (Utrecht case)
findings.consequent: Act in exchange between architect and acoustic consultant, local Environment area not involved
findings.quote: such policies act in the exchange between architect and acoustic consultant, in which the local Environment area is not even involved.

findings.antecedent: Local noise policies/guidelines (Utrecht case)
findings.consequent: Environment area reached agency at a distance, steered integration of noise mitigation requirements without direct involvement
findings.quote: the policies allowed the Environment area to reach agency at a distance, or in other words to steer integration of noise mitigation requirements without being directly involved in the negotiations.

findings.antecedent: Policies become prescriptive (defining minimum dimensions/standards for building design)
findings.consequent: Mitigation solutions acceptable
findings.quote: the policies are not only performance-based, hence defining a noise limit to be reached, but they become prescriptive (Moore and Wilson 2014), defining minimum dimensions and standards to be respected in the building design in order for the mitigation solutions to be acceptable.

findings.antecedent: Requirement transferred from performance-based to prescriptive indications
findings.consequent: Minimum requirements distant from living quality goals
findings.quote: when a requirement is transferred from a performance to a prescriptive indications, this can lead to minimum requirements which are quite distant from the living quality goals that were the original aim of the policy.

findings.antecedent: Too specific prescriptive requirements
findings.consequent: Impossibility of reaching real translation with other requirements, integration of noise mitigation at expense of other requirements
findings.quote: the definition of too specific prescriptive requirements can lead to the impossibility of reaching a real translation with other requirements. In such cases the integration of noise mitigation requirements may happen at the expenses of other requirements

findings.antecedent: Absence of prescriptive indication (noise screen design, Utrecht case)
findings.consequent: Architect defined new solution, successfully integrated noise protection with need for spacious/liveable outdoor areas
findings.quote: the absence of prescriptive indication allowed the architect to define a new solution which could successfully integrate the noise protection requirement with the need for more spacious and liveable outdoor areas.

findings.antecedent: Guidelines providing suggestions of possible design solutions (without prescriptive indications) + flexibility + support interactions
findings.consequent: Enrol designers into process, good balance, architects gain central role
findings.quote: a good balance between providing the needed flexibility and support interactions between practitioners in the definition of mitigation design solutions may be the definition guidelines that provide suggestions of possible design solutions that help enrol designers into the process, without becoming prescriptive indications.

findings.antecedent: Verification modalities of noise levels (in case studies)
findings.consequent: Not 'black-boxed', controversy emerged
findings.quote: verification modalities of the noise levels in this case were not “black-boxed”, as a controversy emerged on the topic.

findings.antecedent: More awareness on verification modalities (how they affect/are affected by actors/design solutions), by all stakeholders (including non-acoustic experts)
findings.consequent: Enhanced careful integration of noise mitigation, informed negotiation between stakeholders
findings.quote: more awareness is needed on verification modalities and how they may affect or beaffected by other actors and design solutions, also by stakeholders that are not acoustic experts. This would enhance the careful integration of noise mitigation aspects in the process and an informed negotiation between stakeholders.

findings.antecedent: Lack of flexibility in policies
findings.consequent: Limit designers in finding solutions for successful integration of different requirements
findings.quote: the lack of flexibility in the policies might limit the designers in finding solutions for a successful integration of different requirements (Bradbury 2016)

findings.antecedent: Performance-based policy (setting maximum noise levels related to life quality standards)
findings.consequent: Avoid abdication in favor of minimum prescriptive requirements for building design, maintain life quality goals
findings.quote: a good solution should be to maintain a performance-based policy, as a general framework, that will pose limits (in this case, maximum noise levels) related to life quality standards that will not be abdicated in favour of minimum prescriptive requirements for the building design.

findings.antecedent: Guidelines providing indications (not prescriptions) on how to respond to noise mitigation requirements through building design
findings.consequent: Enrolment of architect into the process
findings.quote: such policies should be accompanied by guidelines that allow the enrolment of the architect into the process by providing not prescriptions, but indications on how to respond to noise mitigation requirements through building design.

findings.antecedent: Performance-based policies + more flexible descriptive guidelines
findings.consequent: Enhanced role of architects as crucial mediators in the process
findings.quote: The definition of performance-based policies accompanied by more flexible descriptive guidelines will enhance, as said, the role of architects as crucial mediators in the process.

findings.antecedent: Guidelines guiding architects/acoustic consultants in integrating noise mitigation solutions from first steps
findings.consequent: Local offices indirectly act from initial phases, promoting inclusion of mitigation solutions without direct involvement in informal exchanges
findings.quote: The guidelines, by guiding architects and acoustic consultants in integrating noise mitigation solutions from the first steps of the process, will allow local offices to indirectly act from the initial phases of the process, hence promoting the inclusion of mitigation solutions without being directly involved in the informal exchanges between practitioners, in which the design is defined.

findings.antecedent: Use of guidelines (allowing active involvement in design process)
findings.consequent: Enhanced role of acoustic consultants, active involvement in design process, suggesting solutions, supporting architects
findings.quote: The role of acoustic consultants in the process will also be enhanced by the use of guidelines, as it will be possible to be actively involved in the design process (as seen in the Utrecht case study) by suggesting possible solutions and supporting architects in preliminary evaluations.

findings.antecedent: Private practitioners (architects, acoustic consultants) sharing design solutions
findings.consequent: Contribution to evolution of guidelines, dissemination of grey knowledge
findings.quote: Private practitioners such as architects and acoustic consultants may also contribute to the evolution of guidelines, by sharing design solutions developed in specific processes, hence contributing to the much-needed dissemination of grey knowledge put in light by this research.

findings.antecedent: Academic research (systematizing/disseminating findings, conducting new evaluations)
findings.consequent: Support creation of guidelines, enhance pool of solutions, aware evaluation of mitigation results/costs
findings.quote: the efforts of academic research should be directed to support the creation of the guidelines, by systematizing and disseminating findings from existing studies on possible design solutions as well as by conducting new systematic evaluations on new solutions.

findings.antecedent: Researchers' efforts (enhancing/supporting creation of new visual devices, constructed with end-users)
findings.consequent: New visual devices
findings.quote: the efforts of researchers should be used to enhance and support the creation of new visual devices, to be constructed together with the end-users

findings.antecedent: Research taking into account role of citizens/inhabitants (in participatory design in noise polluted areas)
findings.consequent: Better understanding of controversies, improved design processes/policies
findings.quote: research should also consider how to take into account the role of citizens, who are ultimately affected by the choices taken during design processes and policies definition, as they will inhabit the results of such choices.

findings.antecedent: Research methodology (used in this study) + future visualizations
findings.consequent: Applicable to investigation of architecture projects for policies/requirements in any field (e.g., energy saving, lighting, infrastructure)
findings.quote: The research methodology used in this study... could apply to investigation for architecture project with respect to policies and requirements in any field (e.g. energy saving, lighting, lighting, infrastructure requirements and so on).

findings.antecedent: Increasing pool of systematized case studies (categorized by criteria)
findings.consequent: Creation of archive of searchable interactive visualizations
findings.quote: an increasing pool of case studies... should be systematized... allowing the creation of an archive of searchable interactive visualizations

findings.antecedent: Multidisciplinary teams (working on data collection/analysis, digital interactive visualizations)
findings.consequent: Improved research on architecture processes
findings.quote: Similar researches should be conducted into multidisciplinary teams, working on collection and analysis of the information and on the definition of digital interactive visualizations.

findings.antecedent: Constant cooperation and involvement of stakeholders (local offices)
findings.consequent: Stakeholders cooperate in providing archives, periodical evaluations, refinement of visualizations
findings.quote: Such projects should envision constant cooperation and involvement of stakeholders such as local offices. In such vision, the involved stakeholders would not be involved occasionally for interviews and material requests, but they would cooperate in providing archives of possible case-studies as well as in periodical evaluations and refinement of the visualizations.

limitations: Investigation of unpublished studies poses undeniable issues, making it impossible to build an initial literature-based overview of possible case-studies.
Discovery of case studies relies on entering local offices and practitioners’ studios, following their guidance and selection.
Research is a slow process involving many gate-keepers that filter access to information, potentially requiring significant time or leading to closed access.
Difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory and non-partial view of a case study (e.g., Utrecht case where practitioners/developers were inaccessible).
When studies focus on specific controversies, they might remain suspended for months, which can be incompatible with typical research time-spans (e.g., PhD).
Issues of scale of representation emerged, as matters of concern had much shorter duration in the second case study, posing challenges for finding a common scale across different case-studies.
The presentation of maps as completed and static drawings was perceived as a complication in understanding, suggesting a need for interactive maps to select and filter information.
Network visualizations focusing on single moments were evaluated as too complex and potentially counter-productive in preliminary focus groups due to layout differences from general maps.
minimum_safe_summary: This doctoral dissertation investigates noise mitigation in urban transformations from a Science and Technology Studies (STS) perspective, using Actor-Network Theory (ANT) to analyze two case studies in Turin, Italy, and Utrecht, Netherlands. The study develops and evaluates a new visual vocabulary (maps) to represent complex design processes, stakeholder interactions, and policy influences. Key findings highlight that a comprehensive strategy, integrating all requirements early in the process, leads to more successful design modifications and fewer controversies. The research also reveals how policy detail and flexibility influence architects' roles as mediators in integrating noise mitigation solutions. The developed visualizations were found to be legible, effective in promoting new perspectives and interactions among stakeholders, and robust for application across different case studies, though interactive formats are suggested for future improvements. Limitations include challenges in accessing unpublished data, the slow nature of qualitative research with gatekeepers, and issues with the scale and static nature of current visualizations.

mechanism_chain.description: Visualizations improve communication and understanding among stakeholders, leading to more effective collaborative processes in design and policy.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Architectural design and noise mitigation policies are socially constructed, influenced by scientific knowledge, technological capabilities, and societal values, rather than being purely technical or objective endeavors.
